lines.1: With the earth as the lamp's saucer and the vast ocean as its ghee,
lines.2: and the fierce-rayed sun as its flame —
lines.3: I have strung this garland of words at the feet of the red Lord who bears the blazing discus,
lines.4: praying that the ocean of my sorrows may recede.
lines.5: When was it that you churned the ocean, and which world was it whose waters you received in your grasp?
lines.6: I can fathom none of it —
lines.7: is this the same sea you once dammed and breached, the sea on which you now lie sleeping?
lines.8: is this the same earth you made, then dug up, swallowed, and spat out again?
lines.9: One foot you set down to cover the whole earth; with that same foot planted, the earth lay covered —
lines.10: and you stretched on till you reached the very rim of the sea —
lines.11: measuring even the vast, unearthly form of the demon — Great Lord, I cannot fathom it,
lines.12: the way you took that measure.
lines.13: He himself stands as the very gateway and the path — yet, merely barring shut the five sense-doors like the gates of a fortress,
lines.14: can one claim to know him?
lines.15: Even Shiva, who once expounded righteousness to the four sages seated in the shade of the banyan tree,
lines.16: Shiva who holds poison lodged in his throat — even he could not.
lines.17: Hara and Naranan — so their names; the bull is one's mount, the eagle the other's;
lines.18: their canons are the Agamas, his dwelling the eternal Veda; one abides on the rocky peak, the other in the ocean waters;
lines.19: one's work is destruction, the other's is protection and grace; the trident is in one's hand, the discus in the other's;
lines.20: one's form blazes like fire, the other's is the hue of a dark cloud — such is the difference between the two.
lines.21: I have never once forgotten him whose hue is that of the roaring sea —
lines.22: will I forget him today, poor souls that you are? Long ago,
lines.23: lying within the womb, I worshipped him with joined hands, and I saw
lines.24: the very form of the Lord who dwells in sacred Arangam, in every direction.
lines.25: The directions, and the gods who dwell in each direction, and the powers
lines.26: assigned to those gods, and all their several tasks —
lines.27: all these are but the illusion woven by Kannan, the great Lord of unfailing glory, who churned the ocean,
lines.29: Setting your right-whorled conch to your lips till its blast left men bewildered, and hiding away
lines.30: the fierce sun that courses through the sky —
lines.31: why did you do it, O Tirumal, screening it behind your chariot-wheel,
lines.32: and fighting on, the war-discus grasped in your hand?
lines.33: As the boar with tusks made for battle, you plunged in and dug up the earth — and did it not
lines.34: rest then upon that single tusk of yours? Later, stretching wide
lines.35: your blossoming red foot till the directions trembled and the sky shook,
lines.36: you measured that same earth with your vast form.
lines.37: The earth, the mountains, the heaving ocean, the wind,
lines.38: and the very sky — you swallowed them all; so say the wise who have reckoned it well.
lines.39: O glorious one who bears the measureless discus,
lines.40: was this whole world ever large enough to fill your mouth?
lines.41: My mouth will praise none but him; my hands will not join in worship
lines.42: of anyone but him who spanned the world; he who took the demoness's poisoned breast
lines.43: as his food — none but his form and his name
lines.44: will my eyes ever see, or my ears ever hear.
lines.45: Ear, mouth, eye, nose, and body — the five senses; fire,
lines.46: earth, air, water, and sky — the five elements; and beyond these, undying
lines.47: wisdom, sacrifice, and righteous conduct — these, they say,
lines.48: are what befit him who once stood as the boar.
lines.49: That the soul should naturally turn toward the feet of him who wears the cool tulasi garland,
lines.50: and that the immortals should, by their very nature, strive toward that same end —
lines.51: reciting it with right conduct and praising it by fixed observances —
lines.52: he stood there from the very beginning, as the source of it all.
lines.53: Each praises after his own understanding, and each
lines.54: calls some other lord "our own," setting up his image upon the wall,
lines.55: fixing and installing it, they worship it — yet the first, the very source, is
lines.56: none but the form of him who once measured the worlds.
lines.57: The foremost are three; and among those three
lines.58: the foremost is the one whose hue is the surging sea —
lines.59: apart from the grace of that first, good one, in this world ringed by water,
lines.60: the grace of all the other many is worthless.
lines.61: Fearing that so many days had slipped by in vain,
lines.62: I wept — then I saw him upon his serpent-bed, and worshipped:
lines.63: his red eyes closed in sleep while the ocean's waves lapped at his feet —
lines.64: the feet of the red-eyed Lord whose hue is that of the surging sea.
lines.65: His foot crossed beyond the earth, his shoulders spread over the directions,
lines.66: and his crown, they say, measured the very sky — with his sharp claws
lines.67: he tore open Hiranya's chest, and rode upon the great-winged bird,
lines.68: on that day when he measured out the world.
lines.69: He drank the poison from the sagging breast held out to him, and openly
lines.70: stole and ate the butter from the hanging pot; he pressed against the triumphant tusker
lines.71: and fought until it fell, and he split apart the beak of the bird-demon —
lines.72: the same great Lord who crept between the twin trees, and who measured out the earth.
lines.73: O bewildered dark ocean, what penance did you perform, that after swallowing the whole world
lines.74: and sleeping upon a banyan leaf, the Lord of the discus, in his beauty,
lines.75: his dark form and reddened eyes, lies ever asleep upon you,
lines.76: his sacred body forever yours to touch?
lines.77: That his parents' fetters might fall away, he set out in the form of a dwarf,
lines.78: and, red-eyed and great, he strode beyond the domain his enemies had claimed as their own —
lines.79: his red lotus feet, fragrant as young lotus blooms — before them the immortals stand with joined palms,
lines.80: and, standing there, praise him with garlands of full-blown flowers.
lines.81: Standing there, he received the earth poured into his palm, and with his three strides
lines.82: he went forth and measured every direction — that red-eyed Lord's,
lines.83: the discus his weapon, the eagle his mount, the serpent his bed — his feet,
lines.84: O my heart, know them deeply, and hold fast to them.
lines.85: The whole world knows it — I am not the only one who knows it:
lines.86: you, who ride the bright-winged eagle, and you, who ate
lines.87: the butter churned by her of the fragrant, bamboo-soft shoulders —
lines.88: the very rope-marks left on you when she bound you with a cord, for all to see.
lines.89: His beautiful hand still bears the scar left where the string of his bow rubbed against it;
lines.90: his foot still bears the scar from when he kicked apart the demon in the wheel; and there is yet another scar —
lines.91: left when, to the terror of the flower-garlanded goddess, he tore open the chest of the golden-named demon —
lines.92: on the fingers of the Lord whose hue is that of the swelling sea.
lines.93: Seeing the butter smeared over his fingers and his mouth, the cowherd woman
lines.94: bound him tight against the mortar; and on that day, sobbing without pause,
lines.95: brooding and grieving, did you not sit there for all the neighbors to see?
lines.96: Tell me yourself, O Lord whose hue is that of the towering sea.
lines.97: Taking that story to heart, my mind rises unceasingly, at every moment,
lines.98: to praise him — him who lay, like an emerald set upon a mountain, upon the waves,
lines.99: him who tore through the flood, and, becoming a boar, dug up
lines.100: the earth — praising him, my heart rises.
lines.101: Those who rise and take their leave of him who wears the cool tulasi,
lines.102: and those who, thinking on him without fail, worship him daily —
lines.103: for them Venkatam is the hill that quenches the blazing fire of their deeds; and it is the same hill
lines.104: that kindles bright the flame in the hearts of the beings of heaven.
lines.105: He held up a mountain as an umbrella; he tore open the horse-demon's mouth;
lines.106: with his bow he pierced through the seven marA trees; he broke the tusks
lines.107: of the murderous elephant sent to kill him, and he brought down the flowering kurundha tree —
lines.108: all this, the hand that grips the cloud-dark conch.
lines.109: The conch and the discus are in your hands, O cloud-hued Lord;
lines.110: the flower-born goddess dwells forever upon your chest; the red-hued
lines.111: one of the Vedas is born of your navel; and he who shot down the three great fortresses,
lines.112: he too, the proud one, abides as but a small part of your form.
lines.113: He who is water and earth, the vast sky and the wind,
lines.114: the roaring sea and the red fire — he it is, who, when the tusked
lines.115: elephant with the soft green eyes suffered its agony, came and saved it and showered his grace —
lines.116: know this clearly: it is the red-eyed Mal, and none other.
lines.117: Setting the mind straight and clear, through knowledge
lines.118: made clear and well understood, the heart of such a one, with ease,
lines.119: like a calf that seeks out its mother, goes on its own,
lines.120: and finds, and holds fast to, the feet of him who wears the cool tulasi.
lines.121: Holding the conch in one hand and bearing the golden discus in the other,
lines.122: he became both lion and man at once, and tore open the chest
lines.123: of the fire-hued demon — but for the feet of that Lord, is there
lines.124: any other thought that could so much as cross the mind, even for the blink of an eye?
lines.125: Gazing with unblinking eyes till the darkness recedes,
lines.126: and without bending before the five unruly senses that will not be stilled,
lines.127: those who embrace him in their hearts, they alone shall reach
lines.128: the city of him who rests upon the thousand-mouthed serpent.
lines.129: He who, in his grace, gave the four-faced one his dwelling upon the lotus,
lines.130: he whose very names declare and give forth the Vedas —
lines.131: if one merely recites his name and counts the syllables, without truly dwelling on it in the mind,
lines.132: what use is that in the evening rite one performs?
lines.133: Incomparable seers declare it true: that you, who once swallowed all seven worlds and, alone,
lines.134: lay as a child upon a banyan leaf — O cloud-hued one — while your heart did not melt
lines.135: for the false mother who offered her poisoned breast, and she did not survive it — yet at that same encounter,
lines.136: your heart melted for the cowherd mother who truly gave you her breast; such was the way of it.
lines.137: Whatever your devotees say, out of the fullness of their settled love,
lines.138: do not take it, once you have understood it, to be a fault, O Lord;
lines.139: for was it not so that even Ravana of the ten heads gained your feet, O boundless one,
lines.140: through the very enmity that he himself had raised against you?
lines.141: Was it not to destroy his own arrogance and his violence, that of old,
lines.142: you tore Hiranya open — he who claimed this earth as his own —
lines.143: with your sharp, wounding claws — and is this why, O Lord with the golden discus in hand,
lines.144: you later begged for the very earth as alms, and received it so?
lines.145: The learned who have mastered subtle wisdom beyond dispute, every day
lines.146: carrying incense, lamps, and fair water, arrive from every direction —
lines.147: it is at Venkatam that these men of the Vedas come and bow; it is the town that the Lord
lines.148: who once blew the white conch to his lips has taken to his heart and cherished.
lines.149: Where the striped snake glides, and where the bright hill-folk fling great gems
lines.150: to drive off the huge elephants — those very gems, taken for lightning
lines.151: amid the clouds, are sought out by the snakes returning to their holes — that is Venkatam, the place the gods above
lines.152: call their own, and call it the dwelling of their Lord.
lines.153: He dug up the earth; he lifted up the mountain;
lines.154: he strode past Kamsa till that tyrant trembled in fear; and before all this he lay
lines.155: upon the great, wave-tossed ocean — and now the Lord of the surging waters
lines.156: stands, greater still, forever at Venkatam.
lines.157: There, where hunters carry great bows and blazing torches,
lines.158: the elephant flees the hillside fields in terror, and even at the sight of a star
lines.159: falling across the wide sky, it shrinks back in fear — that is Venkatam, the very hill that once rejoiced
lines.160: to see the lord of the demons fall.
lines.161: Even if a fault as huge as a mountain is committed, he takes note only of the good;
lines.162: so from this day forth, O my heart, forever,
lines.163: even if it is but empty, outward praise, keep dwelling
lines.164: on the true praise of him who holds the golden discus in his hand.
lines.165: When the goddess of fortune, the goddess of the earth, and the goddess of the cowherds all come together,
lines.166: why is it that his heart settles wholly on the goddess of fortune alone? — his,
lines.167: who lies upon the hooded serpent's bed while the milky waves break gently near him,
lines.168: the mind of the Lord whose hue is that of the roaring sea.
lines.169: The taint of the mind will vanish, and even the most stubborn deeds will not come near;
lines.170: true wealth of its own accord will come to hand, for those who stand
lines.171: carrying flowers and water to the feet of him who wears the fresh tulasi garland,
lines.172: worshipping — such are those who belong to him.
lines.173: Whatever form his devotees delight in, that very form he himself becomes;
lines.174: whatever name his devotees delight to call him, that name he takes as his own — and however
lines.175: his devotees fix their minds upon him, unwavering, without blinking,
lines.176: in just that way does the Lord of the discus appear to them.
lines.177: Is it even possible for the immortals to know him? Let that question stand —
lines.178: for we ourselves shall come to know him, O my good heart! He upon whose lotus dwells
lines.179: the great ascetic Brahma, who once bowed at his feet — and Ravana's long heads,
lines.180: he counted with his own foot; such is his true nature.
lines.181: Shiva, who took as his begging-bowl the skull of the four-Veda-mastering Brahma,
lines.182: who wears the white sacred thread across his chest — for that sin of his to be undone, before the wounded-hearted Lord —
lines.183: it is those who bow at the feet of that Lord who, mark this,
lines.184: shall both enjoy the bliss of the immortals and rule over this earth.
lines.185: Drawing in the flood, reining in the five maddened elephants of the senses,
lines.186: keeping them from roaming the streets, setting the mind straight — through such
lines.187: true and keen knowledge, those who attain understanding shall behold the feet
lines.188: of him who once, long ago, saved the elephant caught by the crocodile.
lines.189: Seizing one foot with one hand and swinging it round, while on his other hand
lines.190: the whirling blaze made both gods and demons tremble in fear —
lines.191: toward the red feet of him who bore that battle-discus, come,
lines.192: O my sea-deep heart, come with joy.
lines.193: Like a single magizha-seed that takes a different shape each time it is cast, the many bodies the soul assumes
lines.194: will loosen their hold only for those who strive to be free — and even then, the sight of the crown
lines.195: that shines like a blossom just unfolding into radiance, the tall golden crown
lines.196: of our First One, remains hard to attain even for those still seeking it.
lines.197: Restraining the five unruly senses, taking choice flowers, and with the loving heart
lines.198: to embrace him fittingly — held close in this way, he who is so great
lines.199: becomes easy to behold: he who, without turning away, took with generous hand the water of gift
lines.200: poured out by Mahabali as he sat enthroned in splendor.
lines.201: That my mind might easily behold both his feet,
lines.202: it grows clear and settles, quite simply — think, then, of the sacred name
lines.203: of him who, becoming the lion-man, waged war on the one who in his pride
lines.204: would not bow before him, and who sat there having conquered him.
lines.205: The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Adityas, and the two Ashvins together,
lines.206: bearing bright-hued flowers, draw near him every day,
lines.207: and, praising him without pause, at every moment, with a single garland of verse,
lines.208: they go forth and worship with joined hands the Lord of the goddess of fortune.
lines.209: When he walks, the serpent turns into his umbrella; when he sits, into his royal throne;
lines.210: when he stands, into his sandals; and always, out in the vast ocean,
lines.211: it becomes his raft, his jewelled lamp, his flowered silken cloth, the embrace
lines.212: of the very bed that holds Tirumal — such is the serpent.
lines.213: The serpent he danced upon and subdued; the mighty elephant he wrestled down; the crane-demon's beak he tore;
lines.214: he tended the cattle, he threw down wrestlers strong as mountains, hiding nothing of his strength;
lines.215: he uprooted the kurundha tree, he danced the round-dance with the cowherd girls, he ate the butter,
lines.216: and he lifted up the hill — he, the red-eyed one.
lines.217: Whatever sins his own devotees may bear, our Lord
lines.218: simply says, "they are still mine," and lets it be — but the officers of Death,
lines.219: however closely they search and question, will never so much as make out, mark this,
lines.220: the very names of those who have become servants of him of great renown, who reclines upon the serpent.
lines.221: Who indeed can truly know our Lord, beyond merely uttering his name in rapture?
lines.222: Let that question rest — for consider this directly:
lines.223: even Brahma, though he dwells within the fragrant lotus itself,
lines.224: cannot behold the lotus feet of that same Kannan.
lines.225: I feared the harsh deeds that stood so close beside me — in that fear,
lines.226: I sought only to reach your sacred feet, that I might be saved; and with loving devotion,
lines.227: I have taken up the fine garland of words that proclaims "Namo Narayana,"
lines.228: and worshipping, I have learned it by heart.
lines.229: Worship him, take flowers and incense in hand, rise up —
lines.230: may you flourish, O my mind! For one without blemish
lines.231: who learns the sacred mantras and joins hands to worship the feet of Mal,
lines.232: there stands no obstacle at all — go, and reach him.
lines.233: If you wish that the stubborn deeds clinging to you, along with grief, sickness, and sin,
lines.234: all entangled together, should turn back and leave you for good —
lines.235: then take refuge at the feet of him who, long ago, broke the power of Lanka
lines.236: for the sake of the slender-waisted one, and who set his own foot upon that shore.
lines.237: As refuge — together with Brahma, born of the lotus, who brought forth the Vedas —
lines.238: and as shelter against death, for every abiding soul,
lines.239: apart from the Lord who bears the great discus, this world
lines.240: girded by a single ocean, knows no other.
lines.241: The world, and the vast age that stretches on beyond the world, the far dark ocean
lines.242: of gleaming splendor, the mountains that stand within the world,
lines.243: the red fire, the wind, and the sky —
lines.244: all these are but the union brought forth within the very thought of Tirumal.
lines.245: He crept between the close-grown twin trees and brought down the flowering kurundha; to win his fragrant bride
lines.246: he subdued the seven fierce bulls, till the onlookers trembled in fear —
lines.247: and his pervading of the seven worlds, and his going forth through all eight directions —
lines.248: all these are the deeds of the shoulders of him who lies upon the coiled serpent.
lines.249: My two ears bow to none but him;
lines.250: day after day they remain fixed on hearing his sweet words alone;
lines.251: my tongue speaks only of the resounding anklet of him who lies coiled upon the serpent —
lines.252: unashamed, I cling to this alone as my true good.
lines.253: I do not covet what belongs to others; I do not keep company with the base;
lines.254: I find my rise only among the exalted, and beyond that I marvel at nothing;
lines.255: I praise no god as God but Tirumal —
lines.256: how, then, could any sin ever come upon me?
lines.257: They will never be overpowered by their own deeds, nor will they enter the fierce hell;
lines.258: not even the smallest step will they take upon the evil path —
lines.259: those who, with joined hands, worship him who is dark, who is both far and near to thought,
lines.260: him of the thousand names, the red-eyed, dark-hued one.
lines.261: What the world, rising at dawn, studies and comes to know; what the great and foremost scholars of the Veda long for;
lines.262: and what, beside the boundless ocean, is recited and pondered —
lines.263: the feet of him who bears the discus —
lines.264: all this, in the end, is but the name of him who holds the great discus.
lines.265: The tide forever turns toward the dark sea; the bright lotus
lines.266: forever turns toward the risen sun; every living soul
lines.268: and true understanding turns toward that one alone, the consort of the radiant lotus goddess.
lines.269: Who can ever fathom your greatness, age after endless age?
lines.270: Who can ever fathom your very form? Who can fathom it at all —
lines.271: you who dwell in the sky, you who dwell on earth, you who dwell on Venkatam, you who dwell within
lines.272: the very music of the four Vedas — who can fathom the place where you lie?
lines.273: In the form of a child, having swallowed the seven worlds,
lines.274: you once lay and grew upon a banyan leaf — this, they say, is true;
lines.275: tell me, then — did that banyan tree stand within the ocean's waters, or in the sky, or upon the earth?
lines.276: Tell me this, you who lifted up the grove-encircled hill.
lines.277: For as long as you can speak, worship; for as long as this frail body
lines.278: still moves and lasts, praise Tirumal —
lines.279: whether with garlands of fine petals, with sacrifice, with ritual craft, with sacred mantra,
lines.280: or simply with his holy name — if you praise him so, it will be well.
lines.281: Even should one, freed of disease and old age, stand and rule the whole earth
lines.282: through all four ages — even then, do not let go, O my heart!
lines.283: I have sought and desired only this, mark it well:
lines.284: love for him who bears the battling discus.
lines.285: My tongue itself says, "draw near to him, the Lord of the loving discus";
lines.286: it says, "praise and extol the beautiful shoulders of him who was before all time";
lines.287: my eyes say, "behold him whom I have never yet beheld"; my ears say, "listen" —
lines.288: such is the glory of him who wears the jewelled garland.
lines.289: Whether you praise him or find fault with him, whether you scorn him or turn your thoughts to him, O my heart —
lines.290: still he remains what he is: he who took to himself the gleaming
lines.291: ocean, the mountains, the vast sky, the wind,
lines.292: and every body and every soul.
lines.293: He who rode the bull, and he who rides the eagle; he who burned the triple fortress, and he who tore open the demon's chest;
lines.294: he who is smeared with ash, and he whose hue is that of the shadowed gem; he who bears Death himself at his side,
lines.295: and he in whom the two goddesses dwell; he of the long matted locks, and he of the tall crown;
lines.296: he from whose hair the Ganga flows, and he of the resplendent anklet — may they both be our protection.
lines.297: The moment one thinks of him as one's protector, even the most stubborn deeds fall away;
lines.298: the moment one thinks of him, one's bonds loosen and dissolve; old age itself
lines.299: has no hold over those who keep him in their thoughts — O Tirumal,
lines.300: those who come and worship your feet will surely find the way.
lines.301: Those who stand firm upon the path and worship you become, in themselves,
lines.302: the very embodiment of the unfailing Word — and no flaw will ever come near them again;
lines.303: it grants them heaven itself, without fail —
lines.304: such is the glorious Tiruvenkatam of him who measured the earth.
lines.305: At Venkatam, at the heavenly city, at Vehka, and at the flower-filled, unfailing wide golden town of Kovil —
lines.307: he has stood, he has sat, he has lain down, he has walked —
lines.308: merely to say this is enough to destroy every affliction.
lines.309: Who indeed would ever suffer, O my heart — rise!
lines.310: With fresh, freshly-gathered flowers, let us worship with joined hands
lines.311: the feet alone of him who reclines upon the hooded serpent,
lines.312: of him who freed the elephant seized by the cruel, pursuing crocodile.
lines.313: Who indeed would ever blame the one who gave, rather than the one who took?
lines.314: Begging Mahabali, saying only "give me land," as the bright stream
lines.315: of water touched your outstretched hand, did you not then rise up at once,
lines.316: till your very hand came to touch the far reaches of the vast sky?
lines.317: Fleeing, crying, "I cannot bear this cruel, pressing enemy,"
lines.318: the great one, gripped fast by the venomous crocodile lurking in the wide pit,
lines.319: was given the mighty hand of the Lord of wondrous form —
lines.320: could there be anyone who would not become his servant?
lines.321: On that day, amid armies locked in war, seeking his ancient victory,
lines.322: he planted the mountain as his churning-rod, and, winding the long serpent about it,
lines.323: he churned the sea — merely to utter that name, the name of him who churned so,
lines.324: is itself the very weapon that carries one clear of this ancient world.
lines.325: Where sword-eyed women, bearing fresh flower garlands together with fragrant incense,
lines.326: move between the offerings till even the stars seem to vanish, dimmed by the rising smoke —
lines.327: that is Venkatam, the very hill
lines.328: of him who once shot down the illusory golden deer.
lines.329: You held the mountain as your umbrella, your shoulder its handle, to guard the cattle-herds of the cowherd folk;
lines.330: and however was it that you slew those seven fierce bulls? He, mighty as he is,
lines.331: who lies within the deep ocean, rose against the night-roaming demons who dared oppose him —
lines.332: such is the Lord who bears the great discus.
lines.333: O Lord, who else could ever truly know your greatness?
lines.334: On the day you drew near and measured the world in your boar form —
lines.335: I wonder, my Father, how it was that the measure of that single tusk was not enough,
lines.336: so that your very foot itself had to go and take the measure.
lines.337: Do you truly know the ways of this world, O heart? Do you know
lines.338: the eagle-banner of him who reclines upon the serpent? Tell me, then —
lines.339: O heart that stands fixed upon the true path, restraining the five senses within,
lines.340: and bearing flowers and water in hand — do you truly know it?
lines.341: If you and the goddess of fortune stand together — you who lifted the mountain
lines.342: and warded off the driving, freezing rain, O gracious Lord —
lines.343: then at the beautiful, flower-filled town of Kovil, where I can neither pass its gate nor enter within,
lines.344: let me, from now on, simply hold fast to the threshold itself.
lines.345: Who, after this, would ever enter the gate of hell? Rise up!
lines.346: Without hesitation, take firm hold of his ancient feet —
lines.347: of him whose shoulders once flung the calf-demon away like a ripened fruit —
lines.348: so that you may behold his resounding anklet, in this well-known land ringed by nAval groves.
lines.349: If ever I seek anything, it is your feet alone that I shall seek, day after day;
lines.350: if ever I sing, it is your glory alone that I shall sing;
lines.351: if ever I crown myself with anything, it is the golden feet alone of him who bears the golden discus
lines.352: that I shall wear — should it ever be otherwise, what indeed would become of me?
lines.353: Who else, truly, could ever be anyone to me — our Lord,
lines.354: who alone stands as his own protector, and none other?
lines.355: Even the dark kAyAm-flower of the field unfolds and opens, as if to reveal a lovely form —
lines.356: it grants me the boon of glimpsing his own dark, great body.
lines.357: Thinking himself invincible because of the boon he had won,
lines.358: and declaring that never would he bow his head before your feet, O Madhava —
lines.359: for this alone, becoming lion and man in one,
lines.360: you tore apart, with your own strength, the flesh of Hiranya, who had stood as your match in might.
lines.361: Entering within this frail dwelling of flesh, dispelling the darkness,
lines.362: kindling, day after day, the bright flame of true knowledge —
lines.363: for those who do not draw near and cleave to the feet of the eternal Lord
lines.364: who, in the form of the boar, dug up the world — could heaven ever be theirs?
lines.365: You who become the sky, the fire, the heaving ocean, the wind, the very honey and the milk —
lines.367: that once, long ago, spat forth the whole earth,
lines.368: ever be filled just by swallowing the cowherd woman's butter?
lines.369: When he came at you, sword drawn, his belly ablaze with rage, why did you
lines.370: open your gleaming teeth and set your mouth upon him as though in fear — you, whose dotted claws
lines.371: had already torn apart that flower-soft form, O Lord of the golden discus —
lines.372: crushing his very pride to nothing, beneath your red foot.
lines.373: Rising up in fury, his eyes ablaze like fire, opening wide his mouth,
lines.374: he showed, whole and entire, all these seven worlds within it, saying, "these too are mine" —
lines.375: he showed it to the very Brahmins themselves — apart from that dark, great form,
lines.376: my tongue will never, even for an instant, praise anything else.
lines.377: Is there not a tongue in my mouth to say, over and over, "Namo Narayana"?
lines.378: Is there not such speech within me?
lines.379: Is there not, then, a way for me to reach that undying, exalted state?
lines.380: How, then, could I ever take the wicked path?
lines.381: Do not waver, O my heart — behold, it is the red-eyed Mal;
lines.382: he stands as both righteousness and sin, and as the one beyond both, untouched by either;
lines.383: he is this earth, the heaving ocean, and the wind — he himself is the one who came to us —
lines.384: behold this, and hold to it as your very last, unfailing refuge.
lines.385: O great Lord, who once saved the tusked elephant together with its mate —
lines.386: was it not by reaching your very feet that she received your grace —
lines.387: she, the resplendent river called by the golden name of Ganga,
lines.388: whose waters leapt down upon the radiant, ash-smeared locks of Shiva, who holds fire in his palm?
lines.389: The holy one of matted, twisted locks and golden radiance, and the boundless Mal
lines.390: who forever stands pervading the world —
lines.391: though the two may move about, each in his own separate form,
lines.392: still, one of them ever dwells within the very body of the other.
lines.393: He exists — see this, O my good heart — the Supreme One exists forever;
lines.394: he exists, too, within the very hearts of those who dwell on him in thought;
lines.395: he who abides within the great flood, and he who dwells upon Venkatam,
lines.396: is the very one who dwells within the heart — understand and know this.
lines.397: The one foot that kicked apart the demon in the wheel — that bright, flower-like red foot —
lines.398: and both his feet together, you may behold, O my heart:
lines.399: him who, with a single foot, once measured and spanned the world — Kesava, who wears the garland of cool tulasi,
lines.400: that wondrous Lord — keep him alone fixed within your mind.
